planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; this patented sport of Marble Queen is smaller and slower-growing than its parent, so give it a little more light to keep the variegation crisp.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix, since the pale, chlorophyll-poor sectors of the leaves scorch quickly in direct sun but fade toward plain green in dim corners. Leaves are irregularly edged in white with smaller gray-green flecked patches, or "pearls," scattered across the blade, a sport of Marble Queen discovered and patented by a University of Florida breeding program rather than an older heirloom selection. It grows noticeably more compactly and slowly than standard golden or Marble Queen pothos, making it well suited to a small pot, terrarium edge, or tight shelf where a rangier vine would outgrow the space. Let the potting mix dry between waterings and rotate the pot occasionally so light reaches all sides evenly, since uneven light can cause lopsided, thinner growth on the shaded side.
sources: University of Florida IFAS — Epipremnum aureum cultivar releases

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in consistently bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Harlequin carries far more white than green on each leaf, so it needs steadier light and more careful watering than ordinary pothos to avoid stalling out.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in consistently bright, indirect light in well-drained, fast-draining potting mix, since leaves that are mostly white have very little chlorophyll left to drive growth or recover from stress. Harlequin is among the most heavily variegated pothos selections in cultivation, with many leaves emerging almost pure white and marked only with irregular green streaks or blotches, a far more extreme pattern than Marble Queen or N'Joy. Because so little leaf tissue photosynthesizes, growth is slow and any stem that reverts toward solid green should be pruned out promptly so it does not outcompete the variegated portions of the plant. Water more sparingly than a typical pothos, letting the mix dry well between waterings, since the reduced leaf tissue also means the plant uses water more slowly and is easily overwatered.
